prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists.

Write it in this voice: Calm, even register. Mostly medium-length, complete sentences, with length set by content rather than rhythm. No pattern of a short hook paid off by a longer sentence. Plain words over writerly ones, and lines allowed to sit flat. Numbers, names and concrete facts carry the point instead of abstractions. Em dashes, parentheticals, adverbs, doublets and parallelism kept rare. Descriptive writing states what a thing is and does, and any view is labelled as a view. British spelling.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.

text:
When a browser is given an address such as https://example.com/products, its first job is to read the URL and split it into parts. The scheme, https, says which protocol to use and implies port 443. The host, example.com, says which server to contact. The path, /products, says what to ask that server for. Before it does any network work, the browser checks a few local things. It looks at its HSTS list, which records sites that must only be reached over HTTPS, and it looks at its caches. If it holds a fresh stored copy of the page, the request can finish here and nothing is sent over the network.

If no usable copy exists, the browser needs an IP address for the host name. It checks its own DNS cache first, then asks the operating system, which checks its cache and the hosts file. If neither knows the name, the request goes to a recursive resolver, usually run by the ISP or a public provider. The resolver may already have the answer cached. If not, it works down the hierarchy. It asks a root server which servers handle .com, asks those which servers handle example.com, and asks the last of these for the address. The answer comes back with a time-to-live, often a few minutes, which every cache along the way respects. Some browsers send these queries over an encrypted channel, called DNS over HTTPS, instead of plain UDP on port 53. A lookup that has to go all the way down can take tens of milliseconds, and a cached one takes close to none. The result may be an IPv4 address, an IPv6 address, or both, and many browsers try both and use whichever connects first.

With an address in hand, the browser opens a TCP connection to port 443. TCP begins with a three-step handshake. The browser sends a SYN packet, the server replies with SYN-ACK, and the browser answers with ACK. This costs one round trip, so if the server is 40 milliseconds away, the handshake takes about 40 milliseconds before any data can move. Browsers using HTTP/3 skip this step, because that version runs over QUIC on UDP and folds the connection and encryption setup together. The description below follows the more common TCP path.

Next comes the TLS handshake, which sets up encryption and checks who the server is. The browser sends a ClientHello message. It lists the TLS versions and cipher suites it supports, includes the host name in a field called Server Name Indication so that a server hosting many sites knows which certificate to use, and includes its half of a key exchange. In TLS 1.3, which most current sites use, the server answers in a single message. It chooses a cipher suite, sends its half of the key exchange, and sends its certificate chain. Both sides can then compute the same shared secret without it ever crossing the network, and everything after that point is encrypted. TLS 1.3 needs one round trip for this. TLS 1.2 needed two.

The browser then decides whether to trust the certificate. It checks that the host name appears in the certificate's list of names, that the dates are valid, and that the certificate was signed by an authority whose own certificate chains up to one of the root certificates stored in the browser or the operating system. It also checks the signature on each link in the chain. Revocation is checked in various ways, such as stapled OCSP responses from the server or lists the browser keeps. If any check fails, the browser stops and shows a warning page instead of continuing. If the browser has connected to this server before, it may use a session ticket to resume the earlier session. That shortens the handshake, and in TLS 1.3 it can even let the browser send the request alongside the first message.

Once the secure channel exists, the browser can send the HTTP request. Under HTTP/2, which is negotiated during the TLS handshake through a field called ALPN, the request is not plain text. It is a set of headers in a compressed binary format. The essential parts are the method, GET, the path, /products, the authority, example.com, and headers such as Accept, Accept-Encoding and User-Agent. The browser also attaches any cookies it has stored for that site, and a cached copy's validators, ETag or Last-Modified, if it has an expired copy it wants to revalidate. The request is split into frames, encrypted by TLS, split into TCP segments and sent.

On the way, the data may pass through a CDN or a load balancer. These often terminate the TLS connection themselves and forward the request to an origin server over a separate connection. A CDN may answer from its own cache, which saves the trip to the origin. If it cannot, the request goes on to the application server. That server may run code, query a database, render a page, and then start writing a response. A web server often waits until it has the status line and headers ready, and sometimes part of the body, before sending anything.

The first byte of the response is the first piece of that reply to reach the browser. It is carried in a TCP segment, decrypted by TLS, and read as the start of the response headers, for example a status of 200 and a Content-Type of text/html. Developers measure the time up to this point as Time to First Byte. It is the sum of the stages described here: DNS lookup, TCP connection, TLS negotiation, the request travelling to the server, the server's own processing, and the first part of the reply travelling back. In the browser's developer tools, the Network panel shows these stages separately for each request, and looking at them is the most direct way to see which one is slow for a given page.
